'''baptizement''' (bap-tīz′ment), ''n.'' [< ''baptize'' + ''-ment.''] The act of baptizing; baptism. [Rare.]

'''baptizer''' (bap-tī′zėr), ''n.'' One who baptizes.
{{smaller block|On the part of the ''baptizer,'' baptism was a form of reception to instruction.
{{right|''Rees,'' Cyc., Baptism.}}}}

'''baquet''' (ba-kā′), ''n.'' [F.: see ''backet.''] A small tub or trough.

'''bar<sup>1</sup>''' (bär), ''n.'' [< ME. ''barr, barre,'' < OF. ''barre,'' F. ''barre'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. It. ''barra,'' < ML. ''barra,'' of unknown origin. The Celtic words, Bret. ''barren,'' a bar, a branch, W. ''bar,'' a bar, rail, Gael. and Ir. ''barra,'' a bar, spike, Corn. ''bara'' (v.), bar, as well as MHG. ''bar, barre,'' a barrier, G. ''barre,'' Dan. ''barre,'' a bar, ingot, Russ. ''barŭ,'' bar (of a harbor), are from the ML., Rom., or E. Hence ''barrier, barrister, barricade, barrace, embar, embarrass, debar, debarrass,'' etc.] '''1.''' A piece of wood, metal, or other solid matter, long in proportion to its thickness, used for some mechanical purpose; a rod: as, a capstan-''bar;'' the ''bars'' of a grate; the splinter-''bar'' of a vehicle; especially, such a piece of wood or metal used as an obstruction or guard: as, the ''bars'' of a fence or gate; the ''bar'' of a door or window.—'''2.''' Anything which obstructs, hinders, or impedes; an obstruction; an obstacle; a barrier.
{{smaller block|Must I new ''bars'' to my own joy create?
{{right|''Dryden.''}}
The incapacity to breed under confinement is one of the commonest ''bars'' to domestication.
{{right|''Darwin,'' Var. of Animals and Plants, I. 21.}}}}

{{smaller block|Thackeray falls into the common error of describing “a ''bar-sinister''” as a mark of bastardy. A bar in heraldry, being horizontal, cannot be dexter or sinister; a bend may be either.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., III. 46.}}}}

'''Bar super''', in ''apiculture'', a case or crate in which the honeycomb is hung from bars, instead of being built in sections or boxes. ''Phin'', Dict. Apiculture, p. 70.—'''Bastard bar.''' Same as ''baston'', 1 (''c'').—'''Blank bar''', in ''law'', a plea in bar which in an action of trespass is put in to compel the plaintiff to assign the certain place where the trespass was committed; a common bar. It is most used by the practisers in the Common Bench, for in the King’s Bench the place is commonly ascertained in the declaration. ''Blount.''—'''Branchial bar.''' See ''branchial.''—'''Double bar''', in ''music'', two bars placed together at the conclusion of a movement or strain. If two or four dots are added to it, the strain on that side should be repeated.—'''Equalizing-bar.''' (''a'') In a car-truck, a wrought-iron beam which bears upon the top of the journal-boxes on the same side of the truck. The springs which sustain the weight of the body of the car upon that side rest upon the center of this bar, which distributes the weight upon the two journals. (''b'') In a vehicle, a bar to each end of which a whippletree is attached. It is pivoted at the middle, and is used to equalize the draft of two horses harnessed abreast. Also called ''evener'' and ''doubletree.''—'''Father of the bar.''' <noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|baptistic|446|baraket}}</noinclude>''tist.''] Pertaining to baptism, or (with a capital) to the doctrine of the Baptists.

{{smaller block|This ''baptistical'' profession, which he ignorantly laugheth at, is attested by fathers, by councils, by liturgies.
{{right|''Abp. Bramhall'', Schism Guarded, p. 205.}}}}

'''Baptistically''' (bap-tis′ti-kal-i), ''adv.'' According to Baptist doctrine; in the manner of the Baptists.

'''baptizable''' (bap-tī′zạ-bl), ''a.''   [< ''baptize'' + ''-able.'']   That may be baptized. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|As for the condition limiting persons ''baptizable,'' which is actual believing, this also the Church of Christ understood in a limited and temporary sense.
{{right|''Bp. Gauden'', Tears of the Church, p. 284.}}}}

'''baptization†''' (bap-ti-zā′shọn), ''n.''   [< LL. ''baptizatio(n-)'', < ''baptizare'', baptize: see ''baptize.'']   The act of baptizing; baptism. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|If they had been lay persons, their ''baptizations'' were null and invalid. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Clerus Domini, iv.}}}}

'''baptize''' (bap-tīz′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''baptized'', ppr. ''baptizing.''   [< ME. ''baptizen'', < LL. ''baptizare'', < Gr. βαπτίζειν, dip in or under water, baptize, < βάπτειν, dip in water. See etym. of ''baptism.'']   '''1.''' To administer the rite of baptism to. See ''baptism.''

{{smaller block|None [in Yucatan] might marry who had not been ''baptised.'' {{right|''Faiths of the World'', p. 248.}}}}

'''2.''' To christen; name; denominate: with allusion to the naming of infants at baptism.

<poem>Call me but love, and I’ll be new ''baptiz’d'';
Henceforth I never will be Romeo.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 2.}}}} Sometimes spelled ''baptise.''

'''baptizement''' (bap-tīz′ment), ''n.''   [< ''baptize'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of baptizing; baptism. [Rare.]

'''baptizer''' (bap-tī′zėr), ''n.'' One who baptizes.
{{smaller block|On the part of the ''baptizer,'' baptism was a form of reception to instruction.
{{right|''Rees,'' Cyc., Baptism.}}}}

'''baquet''' (ba-kā′), ''n.''   [F.: see ''backet.'']   A small tub or trough.

'''bar<sup>1</sup>''' (bär), ''n.''   [< ME. ''barr, barre,'' < OF. ''barre,'' F. ''barre'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. It. ''barra,'' < ML. ''barra,'' of unknown origin. The Celtic words, Bret. ''barren,'' a bar, a branch, W. ''bar,'' a bar, rail, Gael. and Ir. ''barra,'' a bar, spike, Corn. ''bara'' (v.), bar, as well as MHG. ''bar, barre,'' a barrier, G. ''barre,'' Dan. ''barre,'' a bar, ingot, Russ. ''barŭ,'' bar (of a harbor), are from the ML., Rom., or E. Hence ''barrier, barrister, barricade, barrace, embar, embarrass, debar, debarrass,'' etc.]   '''1.''' A piece of wood, metal, or other solid matter, long in proportion to its thickness, used for some mechanical purpose; a rod: as, a capstan-''bar;'' the ''bars'' of a grate; the splinter-''bar'' of a vehicle; especially, such a piece of wood or metal used as an obstruction or guard: as, the ''bars'' of a fence or gate; the ''bar'' of a door or window.—'''2.''' Anything which obstructs, hinders, or impedes; an obstruction; an obstacle; a barrier.
{{smaller block|Must I new ''bars'' to my own joy create?
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The incapacity to breed under confinement is one of the commonest ''bars'' to domestication.
{{right|''Darwin,'' Var. of Animals and Plants, I. 21.}}}} '''3.''' A barrier—(''a'') At the entrance to a city, or between the city proper and its suburbs; hence, the gate at which the barrier was placed in former times, as Temple ''Bar'' in London, now
removed, and the existing medieval ''bars'' of York. (''b'') At a toll-house; a toll-gate. Also called ''toll-bar.''—'''4.''' An accumulation forming a bank obstructive to navigation or to the flow of water. {{smaller|(''a'') A bank of sand, gravel, or earth forming a shoal in any body of water; a bank or shoal at the mouth of a river or harbor, obstructing entrance or rendering it difficult.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He rose at dawn, and, fired with hope,
Shot o’er the seething harbour ''bar.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Sailor Boy.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') A narrow point of land jutting out into the water. (''c'') In ''placer-mining'', an accumulation of sand or gravel in or near the bed of a stream.}}
—'''5.''' In ''law'': (''a'') The railing inclosing the place which counsel occupy in courts of justice. [Hence the phrase ''at the bar of the court'' signifies in open court.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Some at the ''bar'' with subtlety defend,
Or on the bench the knotty laws untie. ''Dryden.''</poem>}}
(''b'') The place in court where prisoners are stationed for arraignment, trial, or sentence.
{{smaller block|<poem>The great duke
Came to the ''bar;'' where to his accusations
He pleaded still, not guilty. ''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., ii. 1.</poem>}}
(''c'') The practising members of the legal profession in a given community; all those who have the right to plead in a court; counsel or barristers in general, or those present in court.
{{smaller block|It is the bench, the magistracy, the ''bar'' — the profession as a profession . . . — a class, a body, of which I mean exclusively to speak.
{{right|''R. Choate'', Addresses, p. 137.}}}}
{{smaller block|The storm of invective which burst upon him from ''bar'', bench, and witness-box.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., iv.}}}}
(''d'') A stoppage or defeat in an action or suit by countervailing the alleged right of action.—'''6.''' In England, a railing or barrier which separates a space near the door from the body of either house of Parliament, beyond which none but members and clerks are admitted. {{smaller|At these bars counsel stand when pleading before the house, and to the same bar witnesses and such as have been ordered into custody for breaches of privilege are brought. In the houses of Congress, the bar, for the latter purpose, is the area in front of the presiding officer.}}
'''7.''' Figuratively, any tribunal: as, the ''bar'' of public opinion; the ''bar'' of God.—'''8.''' That portion of a tavern, inn, coffee-house, or the like, where liquors, etc., are set out; the counter over which articles are served in such an establishment.
{{smaller block|I was under some apprehension that they would appeal to me; and therefore laid down my penny at the ''bar'', . . . and made the best of my way to Cheapside.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 403.}}}}
'''9.''' A band or stripe: as, a ''bar'' of light.
{{smaller block|The long, slender ''bars'' of cloud float like fishes in the sea of crimson light. {{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}}
'''10.''' In ''farriery'', the upper part of the gums of a horse between the grinders and tusks, which bears no teeth, and to which the bit is fitted.—'''11.''' In ''music'', a line drawn perpendicularly across the staff, dividing it into equal measures of time and marking the place of the strong
accent; hence, the space and notes included between two such lines; the portion of music represented by the included notes. See also ''double bar'', below. {{smaller block|Whistling a random ''bar'' of Bonny Doon.
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Brook.}}}}
'''12.''' In ''com.'': (''a'') An ingot, a lump, or a wedge, as of gold or silver, from the mines, run in a mold, and unwrought. (''b'') A short piece of bar-iron about half a pound in weight, used as a medium of traffic with African negroes.—'''13.''' In ''printing'': (''a'') The lever by which the pressure is applied in a hand-press. (''b'') The middle cross-piece of a printers’ chase.—'''14.''' In ''her.'', a horizontal stripe crossing the field, narrower than the fesse, and occupying usually one fifth or less of the field: one of the nine ordinaries. {{smaller|It is rare that one bar only is used; bars may be borne in any number, and the blazon always names the number; but when more than four, as they are smaller, they are called ''barrulets.'' See ''barry''<sup>2</sup> and ''barwise.''}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0472 c2f2.png|width=104px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Heraldic Bar.}}}} '''15.''' In a bridle, the mouthpiece connecting the checks.—'''16.''' In a rifle-sight, a plate in the form of a segment, with its upper or chord edge horizontal, and secured in a ring. {{smaller|If the plate has a vertical slot in it, it is called a ''slit bar-sight''; if it has an annulus or smaller ring attached to it, it is a ''bar-sight'' or ''open bead-sight.''}} '''17.''' In ''saddlery'', one of the side pieces connecting the pommel and cantle of a saddle.—'''Accented parts of a bar.''' {{smaller|See ''accent'', ''v. t.''}}—'''Bar of ground,''' {{smaller|a term used in Cornwall, England, and elsewhere to designate a stratum or mass of rock coming near to or crossing the lode, and of a different character from that adjacent to it.}}—'''Bar sinister,''' {{smaller|a phrase erroneously used for ''bend sinister.'' See ''bend''<sup>2</sup>.}}

'''bar<sup>1</sup>''' (bär), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''barred'', ppr. ''barring.''   [< ME. ''barren'', < OF. ''barrer'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''barrar'', < ML. ''barrare'', bar; from the noun.]   '''1.''' To fasten with a bar, or as with a bar.
{{smaller block|Every door is ''barr’d'' with gold, and opens but to golden keys.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now to all hope her heart is ''barred'' and cold.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Blind Girl of Castèl-Cuillè, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To hinder; obstruct; prevent; prohibit; restrain.
{{smaller block|<poem>If you cannot
''Bar'' his access to the king, never attempt
Anything on him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The houses of the country were all scattered, and yet not so far off as that it ''barred'' mutual succour.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Though the law of arms doth ''bar''
The use of venom’d shot in war.</poem>
{{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras.}}}}
'''3.''' To except; exclude by exception.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nay, but I ''bar'' to-night; you shall not gage me
By what we do to-night.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 2.}}}}
'''4.''' To provide with a bar or bars; mark with bars; cross with one or more stripes or lines.
{{smaller block|<poem>A Ceynt she wered, ''barred'' al of silke.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|He ''bars'' his surfaces with horizontal lines of colour, the expression of the level of the Desert.{{right|''Ruskin.''}}}}
